entities.name: Perdiccas III of Macedon
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Perdiccas III of Macedon (reigned 365–360 BCE) was king of the Argead dynasty and the elder brother of Philip II, whose death in battle transformed Macedonian history and inadvertently enabled the rise of Alexander the Great.

Coming to power after his brother Alexander II's assassination (365 BCE), Perdiccas faced a kingdom beset by rivals and constant Illyrian pressure on Macedonia's western frontier. He ruled for five years, managing the complex regional politics of northern Greece while struggling to maintain the loyalty of the Macedonian nobility. His younger brother Philip served in his court after returning from Theban exile.

His reign ended catastrophically in 360 BCE when he led the Macedonian army against the Illyrian king Bardylis at the Battle of the Lyncestian plain and was killed along with approximately 4,000 soldiers — more than a third of Macedonia's entire military strength. The disaster left his infant son Amyntas IV as nominal heir. Philip II, then approximately 23 years old, stepped in as regent and seized the throne, rebuilt the Macedonian army with the revolutionary sarissa-equipped phalanx, and crushed Bardylis at the Battle of Erigon Valley in 358 BCE. Perdiccas III's catastrophic defeat thus became, paradoxically, the catalyst that transformed Macedonia from a vulnerable buffer state into the dominant power of the Greek world.
